lessonTitle: HIV Infection: Testing, Opportunistic Disease and Antiretroviral Therapy

blocks.text: A 34-year-old man attends with three weeks of fever, sore throat, a faint trunk rash, mouth ulcers and swollen neck glands that began two weeks after condomless sex with a new partner. His glandular-fever screen is negative. A single blood test will change the next hour of his life, and how you explain what it means matters as much as the result.

blocks.markdown: **Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)** is a retrovirus that infects CD4-positive T lymphocytes (and macrophages) and, untreated, progressively destroys cell-mediated immunity. It is transmitted by sexual contact, blood (injecting equipment, transfusion of unscreened blood), and from mother to child in pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding. After infection there may be an **acute seroconversion illness** (fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers), then a long clinically quiet phase during which viral replication continues and CD4 cells fall, and finally symptomatic immunodeficiency with opportunistic disease (AIDS).

blocks.title: Viral load and CD4 count
blocks.text: **CD4 count** (cells per microlitre of blood) measures the immune damage: lower values mean greater susceptibility to opportunistic infection. **Viral load** (HIV RNA copies per millilitre of plasma) measures viral replication and therefore treatment response and infectiousness. CD4 count tells you how much harm has been done; viral load tells you whether the virus is currently being controlled. Reference thresholds vary by laboratory and guideline.

blocks.markdown: **Testing.** The standard screening test in the UK is a laboratory **fourth-generation combined antigen/antibody assay**, which detects HIV-1/2 antibodies and the p24 antigen. Because p24 antigen appears before antibodies, it shortens the window period. The window period is the time between acquiring infection and a test becoming reliably positive; for fourth-generation tests this is typically a matter of weeks (check current BHIVA/UKHSA advice), so a negative test soon after exposure may need repeating. A reactive screen is confirmed on a further sample according to local protocol. Point-of-care and self-testing kits exist but have longer window periods. At diagnosis the baseline work-up includes CD4 count, viral load, HIV genotypic resistance testing, hepatitis B and C serology, and screening for other sexually transmitted infections and tuberculosis. Pre- and post-test counselling is brief and non-judgemental, and informed consent for testing is part of routine practice.

blocks.caption: Viral load responses are expressed as log10 reductions; a fall of 1 log10 is a ten-fold fall in copies per mL.

blocks.title: Reading a viral load response
blocks.prompt: A patient starts antiretroviral therapy with a viral load of 100 000 copies/mL. Four weeks later it is 1000 copies/mL. What is the log reduction and what does it imply?

steps.text: Compute the log10 of each value.
A 2 log10 fall means the viral load is 100-fold lower, which is a good early response, but 1000 copies/mL is still far above the target.

Most guidelines aim for a viral load below the assay limit of detection (commonly below 50 copies/mL) within about 6 months; the next step is to continue therapy, reinforce adherence and recheck, not to change drugs yet.

blocks.answer: A 2 log10 fall (100-fold) is an encouraging early response; continue treatment and monitor until the viral load is undetectable.

rows: Cerebral toxoplasmosis in those with positive Toxoplasma IgG; cryptococcal disease
Co-trimoxazole also protects against toxoplasmosis; screen for cryptococcal antigen in some settings
CMV retinitis; disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex
Ophthalmic review; MAC prophylaxis is not usually needed if ART is started promptly
blocks.caption: Thresholds are approximate and guideline-dependent (check current BHIVA and local protocols).

blocks.markdown: **Opportunistic infections** are infections that rarely cause serious disease in people with intact immunity. Common ones are PJP, oral and oesophageal candidiasis, tuberculosis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, CMV retinitis and malignancies such as Kaposi sarcoma and lymphoma. Preventing them has two prongs: **primary prophylaxis** (drug given to prevent a first episode when CD4 falls below a threshold) and **starting ART promptly**, which restores CD4 count and usually allows prophylaxis to stop once the count has risen and stayed above threshold on treatment.

blocks.title: When is prophylaxis considered?
blocks.prompt: A 41-year-old woman newly diagnosed with HIV has a CD4 count of 85 cells/microlitre, is asymptomatic and Toxoplasma IgG positive. Which prophylaxis is considered, and why?

steps.text: The CD4 count is below 200, the level at which risk of PJP rises sharply, so co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is considered (dose per BNF and local protocol).
CD4 below 100 with positive Toxoplasma IgG adds a risk of reactivation of latent cerebral toxoplasmosis. Co-trimoxazole also provides protection against this.
She has no symptoms, so she does not have active disease; prophylaxis targets the first episode, not treatment of an existing infection.
ART is started as soon as practicable, and co-trimoxazole is stopped later once her CD4 count has risen above the guideline threshold and remained there while on suppressive treatment.

blocks.answer: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis covers both PJP and toxoplasmosis; ART is the definitive protection because it restores immunity.

blocks.markdown: **Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART)** uses at least three active drugs from at least two classes. A typical initial regimen in the UK combines two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) with an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI); regimens change, so check current BHIVA guidance. Combination therapy is used for the same reason as in tuberculosis: HIV replicates rapidly and its reverse transcriptase is error-prone, so single drugs rapidly select resistant virus. ART is recommended for everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count. The goals are sustained viral suppression, immune recovery and prevention of transmission. Lifelong adherence is essential; viral rebound suggests missed doses, drug interactions, or resistance and prompts resistance testing.

items: Treatment as prevention: a person on ART with a sustained undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV sexually (often written U=U).
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP): antiretroviral drugs taken by HIV-negative people at risk.
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): a short antiretroviral course started as soon as possible after a significant exposure, ideally within 72 hours (follow current BHIVA/UKHSA guidance).
Condoms, needle-exchange programmes, and regular testing for those at risk.
Preventing vertical transmission: maternal ART with suppressed viral load, appropriate mode of delivery, infant prophylaxis and infant-feeding advice.
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS): paradoxical worsening of a latent or treated infection after starting ART; recognise it rather than stop ART.

blocks.title: What the two numbers tell you
blocks.text: CD4 count drives the risk of opportunistic infection and the need for prophylaxis; viral load tracks treatment success and infectiousness. The aim of ART is an undetectable viral load, after which the CD4 count recovers and transmission risk becomes negligible.

points: HIV is diagnosed with a fourth-generation antigen/antibody test, interpreted with the window period in mind; CD4 count measures immune damage and viral load measures viral replication.
Opportunistic infections such as PJP, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal disease and CMV rise as CD4 falls; prophylaxis is considered below approximate thresholds and ART is the definitive protection.
Combination ART with at least three active drugs prevents resistance, suppresses viral load and prevents sexual transmission; PrEP, PEP, condoms and maternal ART complete prevention.

questions.stem: An emergency department is setting up opt-out HIV testing and must choose a laboratory assay. Why is a fourth-generation combined antigen/antibody HIV test preferred to an antibody-only test for this programme?

options.text: Because it detects p24 antigen that appears before antibodies, shortening the window period
Because it measures the CD4 count directly
Because it measures the viral load accurately
Because it is not affected by the window period at all

questions.correctOptionText: Because it detects p24 antigen that appears before antibodies, shortening the window period

distractorRationale.a: Correct: p24 antigen appears earlier than antibodies.
distractorRationale.b: It does not measure CD4 count; that is a separate flow-cytometry test.
distractorRationale.c: Quantitative viral load is a separate RNA test.
distractorRationale.d: All tests have a window period; fourth-generation tests only shorten it.

questions.explanation: Fourth-generation assays detect both HIV-1/2 antibodies and p24 antigen. Because antigen appears before the antibody response matures, these tests detect infection earlier, although a negative result very soon after exposure may still need repeating.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV has a CD4 count of 150 cells/microlitre and 3 weeks of progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough. Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse interstitial shadowing and his oxygen saturation falls on walking. Which opportunistic infection is most likely, and what prophylaxis would have reduced the risk?

options.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; co-trimoxazole
Cytomegalovirus retinitis; ganciclovir
Cerebral toxoplasmosis; pyrimethamine
Cryptococcal meningitis; fluconazole

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CD4 below 200, dry cough, exertional desaturation and bilateral interstitial shadowing are typical of PJP; co-trimoxazole is first-line prophylaxis.
distractorRationale.b: CMV retinitis affects vision at CD4 below about 50, not lungs in this way.
distractorRationale.c: Toxoplasmosis presents with focal neurology or headache, not lung disease.
distractorRationale.d: Cryptococcal disease usually presents with meningitis at lower CD4 counts.

questions.explanation: Dry cough, exertional breathlessness and diffuse bilateral shadowing with a CD4 count below 200 is the classic PJP picture. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended below approximate CD4 thresholds (check current BHIVA guidance).

questions.stem: A man started on ART 8 months ago has a viral load of 40 copies/mL at 6 months, but a repeat now shows 8000 copies/mL. He admits missing tablets for several weeks. What is the most appropriate first approach?

options.text: Stop ART immediately to prevent resistance
Discuss adherence barriers, check drug interactions, and send a viral load with resistance testing if viraemia persists, rather than switching blindly
Add a fourth antiretroviral drug without any testing
Reassure him that fluctuations of this size are normal

questions.correctOptionText: Discuss adherence barriers, check drug interactions, and send a viral load with resistance testing if viraemia persists, rather than switching blindly

distractorRationale.a: Stopping therapy allows viral rebound and further CD4 decline.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: viral rebound after missed doses needs an adherence review and resistance testing before choosing a new regimen.
distractorRationale.c: Adding drugs without a resistance profile does not address the cause and may add toxicity.
distractorRationale.d: A rise to 8000 copies/mL is a significant virological failure, not a minor blip.

questions.explanation: Viral rebound on ART is most often caused by non-adherence, but drug interactions, malabsorption and resistance must be considered. Adherence support and resistance testing guide the choice of any regimen change.

questions.stem: Which statement about preventing HIV transmission is correct?

options.text: A person on effective ART with a sustained undetectable viral load has no risk of sexual transmission
PEP is effective if started any time within a month of exposure
Pre-exposure prophylaxis is only for people already living with HIV
Condoms are unnecessary for people taking PrEP in all circumstances

questions.correctOptionText: A person on effective ART with a sustained undetectable viral load has no risk of sexual transmission

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the principle that undetectable equals untransmittable.
distractorRationale.b: PEP should be started as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours; efficacy falls with delay.
distractorRationale.c: PrEP is for HIV-negative people at risk of acquiring HIV.
distractorRationale.d: PrEP does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections, so condoms still have a role.

questions.explanation: Sustained viral suppression on ART eliminates sexual transmission risk. PEP and PrEP are for HIV-negative people, and neither replaces condoms for protection from other infections.

questions.stem: Which finding best reflects how much immune damage HIV has caused?

options.text: Fall in CD4 count
Presence of a rash at seroconversion
Positive antibody test
Higher haemoglobin

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CD4 count measures the depletion of helper T cells and the degree of immunodeficiency.
distractorRationale.b: The seroconversion rash is a transient feature of acute infection and does not quantify damage.
distractorRationale.c: A positive antibody test indicates infection, not its severity.
distractorRationale.d: Haemoglobin is not a measure of HIV-related immune damage.

questions.explanation: CD4 count is the main marker of immune competence and risk of opportunistic infection, while viral load measures replication. Antibody tests only establish infection.

questions.stem: A single negative fourth-generation HIV test taken 10 days after a high-risk exposure reliably excludes infection.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The window period means a test taken very soon after exposure can be negative even though infection has occurred. A repeat test after the recommended interval is needed, and PEP should be considered if the exposure was recent.

questions.stem: A patient's viral load falls from 400 000 copies/mL before ART to 400 copies/mL after 8 weeks. What is the log10 reduction (give the answer as a number of log10 units)?
questions.explanation: $\log_{10}(400000)=5.602$ and $\log_{10}(400)=2.602$. The difference is 3.0 log10, equivalent to a 1000-fold fall in viral load.

questions.stem: Describe how a new diagnosis of HIV is confirmed and staged, and explain what the CD4 count and viral load each tell you.
markingGuide: Fourth-generation combined antigen/antibody test; reactive result confirmed on a further sample per protocol
Window period concept and repeating a negative test if exposure was recent
Baseline CD4 count, viral load, resistance genotype, hepatitis B/C serology, STI and TB screening
CD4 count measures immune damage and opportunistic infection risk
Viral load measures replication, treatment response and infectiousness
Clinical staging uses symptoms and opportunistic diseases (WHO stages)
questions.explanation: Diagnosis requires a validated screening and confirmation algorithm. The two monitoring numbers answer different clinical questions: how damaged is the immune system, and is the virus being controlled.

questions.stem: Name four opportunistic infections or malignancies in HIV and explain when prophylaxis is considered and why starting ART is the definitive protection.
markingGuide: Any four of: PJP, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, CMV retinitis, TB, candidiasis, MAC, Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma
Risk rises as CD4 falls; PJP prophylaxis considered when CD4 below about 200
Toxoplasma prophylaxis considered at lower CD4 in IgG-positive people; co-trimoxazole covers both
Thresholds vary and must be checked against current guidance
ART restores CD4 count so prophylaxis can later be stopped
Prophylaxis is a bridge, not a substitute for ART
questions.explanation: Opportunistic disease tracks the CD4 count. Prophylaxis buys time, but only immune reconstitution on ART removes the underlying risk.

questions.stem: Explain the principles of combination ART and list the strategies used to prevent HIV transmission.
markingGuide: At least three active drugs from at least two classes; typically two NRTIs plus an INSTI (regimens vary)
Combination prevents rapid selection of resistant virus because HIV replicates fast with an error-prone reverse transcriptase
Lifelong adherence; viral rebound requires adherence review and resistance testing
Goals: undetectable viral load, immune recovery, no sexual transmission
Prevention: U=U, PrEP, PEP as soon as possible (ideally within 72 hours), condoms, testing, prevention of vertical transmission
IRIS may occur after starting ART and should be recognised
questions.explanation: ART works because multiple drugs limit the emergence of resistance. Prevention uses both treatment of those infected and protection of those at risk.
